paras: The whipping of a Fort Valley prisoner was an assault in Georgia in October 1880 in which unidentified men took a Black man accused of theft from a constable, whipped him to force a confession, and left him tied to a tree in front of the Fort Valley guardhouse. The episode reached the press only as the reported cause of a threat to burn Fort Valley, and the local paper that described it said its only evidence was the prisoner's own statement.

According to the Fort Valley Mirror, the man, whom no paper named, had been arrested for stealing "a lot of money" from a Mr. Watson of Crawford County. He was first held in the Fort Valley guardhouse and then handed over to the authorities of Crawford County.

While a constable was taking him to Knoxville, the Mirror reported, he was taken away from the officer and "whipped and otherwise maltreated, to make him confess and return the money." By the prisoner's account, his captors then brought him back to Fort Valley, tied him to a tree in front of the guardhouse, and told him to tell whoever released him that he was not guilty. The papers give no date, place or number of captors for the whipping, and they do not describe his injuries.

On a Tuesday night soon after, persons "supposed to be negroes" left lightwood splinters and matches at every store door and gatepost in Fort Valley, which the Mirror read as a threat to burn the town. The Mirror said that "several negroes" gave the whipping as the cause, though it called that cause only "supposed." No report of an arrest, inquiry or prosecution for the whipping appears in the coverage, and the prisoner's later fate is not reported.

The story began as a Fort Valley Mirror item, which the Savannah Morning News and the Macon Georgia Weekly Telegraph reprinted in full in their state columns on October 29, 1880. The Atlanta Weekly Constitution ran the same text on November 2 under the headline "An Outrage," and the Eastman Times printed a shortened version on November 4 that omitted the word "whipped" and the prisoner's parting message.

The Mirror reserved the word "outrage" for the lightwood threat, while it handled the whipping conditionally: "if it is true," it said, it showed "a contemptible spirit" in men from outside the county who sought "to saddle their misdeeds on Fort Valley." Its concern was the town's reputation, and it insisted that the offense, if committed, had been done "by citizens not of our county." The Summerville Gazette's digest of November 4 dropped these caveats and stated plainly that the threat was "made by negroes in a spirit of revenge" because the prisoner had been taken from the guard and whipped.

accounts.label: Fort Valley Mirror
accounts.gist: Reported the lightwood threat as the work of persons 'supposed to be negroes' retaliating for the whipping, said it had no evidence of the whipping but the prisoner's word, and insisted the offense, if committed, was by men from outside its county.

accounts.label: Summerville Gazette digest
accounts.gist: Stated as fact that the lightwood was a threat 'made by negroes in a spirit of revenge' because the prisoner was taken from the guard and whipped.

framing.detail: The Mirror labeled the lightwood threat 'this outrage' and called the whipping, 'if it is true', evidence of 'a contemptible spirit' in those who would 'saddle their misdeeds on Fort Valley'.
The Atlanta Weekly Constitution reprinted the Mirror item under the headline 'An Outrage'; the Eastman Times ran a shortened version.
The Summerville Gazette's one-paragraph digest dropped the Mirror's caveats and presented the threat as Black revenge for the whipping.
